title: The Purpose You Made Me For

sections.heading: Remembering why I am here
sections.text: Lord, you are the giver of my life and the Lord over all of it. Please make this the deepest concern of my heart: that I would live for the purpose you made me for—to honor you with my whole life and to do whatever good I can for the people around me. If my days are spent without that, I am wasting the life you have given me.
theological_themes: Human life has a God-given purpose.
God is glorified not only by worshipful words but by a whole life directed toward him.
Love of neighbor and usefulness to others belong to faithful obedience.

scripture_references.connection: Paul teaches that even ordinary acts are to be done for God’s glory, which directly supports the prayer’s desire for a whole life aimed at honoring God.
This passage presents believers as created in Christ for good works prepared by God, grounding the prayer’s desire to do real good for others as part of God’s purpose.

sections.heading: Seeing through what people chase
sections.text: Father, I see how easily people build their lives around themselves. I see it in the world, and I see the same pull in me. We chase money, recognition, comfort, entertainment, and the feeling of being important, as if these things could make an eternal soul truly happy. Wake me up from that lie before I give my heart to it.
theological_themes: Self-centered living is spiritually dangerous and deceptive.
Created things cannot bear the weight of ultimate happiness.
The soul was made for God, not for wealth, status, or pleasure as final ends.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus warns that life does not consist in possessions and tells of a man who stored up wealth while neglecting God, matching the prayer’s concern about mistaking earthly gain for true security.
Jesus’ question about gaining the world and losing the soul speaks directly to the prayer’s contrast between worldly success and the well-being of the immortal soul.

sections.heading: Wanting the happiness that is actually real
sections.text: Teach me to believe, deep down, that my happiness is found in loving you and becoming holy because you are holy. Do not let me settle for a life that looks full but is empty of you. Make me want what is clean, lasting, and true more than what is loud, impressive, and temporary.
theological_themes: True blessedness is found in loving God.
Holiness is not opposed to happiness but belongs to it.
God’s people are called to reflect his holiness.

scripture_references.connection: Peter grounds the believer’s call to holiness in God’s own holiness, supporting the prayer’s request to become holy as part of life’s true good.
The psalm locates fullness of joy in God’s presence, illuminating the prayer’s claim that lasting happiness is found in God rather than in created pleasures.

sections.heading: Asking not to be pulled into the world’s emptiness
sections.text: Please keep me from absorbing the attitudes, cravings, and foolishness of a world that lives as though you are not there. When I am tempted by sinful pleasure, easy profit, reputation, or the dream of making a name for myself, help me call it what it is: a false promise. My life is short. The things that look so solid now pass like mist. Do not let me trade my soul for bubbles and wind.
theological_themes: The fallen world system tempts believers away from God.
Earthly life is brief, and worldly pleasures are unstable and unable to satisfy.
Believers need grace to reject sinful gain, pride, and sensuality.

scripture_references.connection: John contrasts love for the world’s desires and pride with doing God’s will, which fits the prayer’s plea to resist vanity, sensuality, and worldly ambition.
James describes human life as brief and passing, supporting the prayer’s sober view of time and its warning against treating temporary things as ultimate.
Ecclesiastes repeatedly exposes life pursued apart from God as unable to satisfy, which helps frame the prayer’s images of emptiness without denying the goodness of God’s creation.

sections.heading: Staying close to you through Christ
sections.text: Give me grace to stay faithful to you—not as someone who can keep myself, but as someone held by your mercy. Keep me close to you, trusting your promises and turning away from whatever competes with you. And keep teaching me that I cannot find real joy, or fulfill your purpose for my life, apart from life in and for your beloved Son, Jesus Christ.
theological_themes: Faithfulness to God depends on grace.
The believer lives in covenant relationship with God by trusting his promises and rejecting rivals.
Life’s purpose and true happiness are found only in Christ.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus teaches that fruitfulness depends on abiding in him, which grounds the prayer’s confession that God’s purpose cannot be fulfilled apart from the Son.
Paul describes the Christian life as life lived by faith in the Son of God, supporting the prayer’s final emphasis on living in and for Christ.
Jude praises God as the one able to keep believers, which supports the prayer’s dependence on grace rather than self-reliance for faithfulness.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original’s statement that life is not worth having unless used for God’s glory and others’ good could be heard as denying the inherent value of human life. This adaptation preserves the force as a warning against wasting God-given life, not as a claim that life loses its created dignity.

The original’s severe language about the present world as sorrowful, empty, and delusive can be misunderstood as rejecting the goodness of creation. This adaptation treats the target as the fallen world system and life pursued apart from God, not the created world as such.
significant_interpretive_choices: “Great name here or hereafter” was rendered as the desire for reputation, legacy, or making a name for oneself, since the original seems to reject both present fame and future human remembrance as ultimate aims.
“Keep in covenant with thee” was expressed as staying faithful to God, trusting his promises, and being held by grace, rather than as a formal covenant-renewal practice.
“Life lived in and for the Son of thy love” was retained as explicitly Christ-centered language, with the relational phrase made contemporary as life in and for God’s beloved Son, Jesus Christ.
